name: Losar at Ghoom
summary: Losar, the Tibetan New Year, is marked in the monasteries of Ghoom and in Tibetan and Sherpa homes across Darjeeling. Expect butter lamps, new prayer flags, family visits, khapse biscuits and prayers at Yiga Choeling. The date follows the lunar calendar and moves each year.
body: Losar falls on the first day of the first month of the Tibetan lunar calendar, usually in February or early March. In Darjeeling it belongs to the Tibetan, Sherpa, Bhutia and Tamang families of the hills, and to the monasteries. Ghoom, with Yiga Choeling (founded 1850), Samten Choling and the Sakya monastery within walking distance of each other, is the easiest place to see its religious side. Many Darjeeling families also mark Sonam Losar or Tamu Lhosar at other times of year, so ask which New Year a monastery is celebrating.

The days before Losar are for cleaning houses and monasteries and for the rites that close the old year; in some monasteries this includes masked cham dances, though which monastery dances in a given year varies. On Losar itself families visit the gompa early, offer khatas and butter lamps, and raise new prayer flags. Homes fry khapse, crisp twisted biscuits, and serve chang and butter tea to guests. The pace is unhurried and visitors are generally welcome to stand quietly at the back.

For visitors this is a quiet, respectful festival rather than a show. Mornings at the monasteries are the time to go. February is cold in Ghoom, around 2,258 m, with clear days and frosty nights, and hotel rates are lower than in spring. Dates and any public programmes change every year, so check current status before you travel. Book a heated room in Darjeeling or Ghoom and walk to the monasteries after breakfast.
tips: Reach the Ghoom monasteries early in the morning, when families come to pray and offer khatas.
Walk clockwise around shrines and prayer wheels, and ask before photographing monks or people at prayer.
Pack for frost: Ghoom in February drops below freezing at night.

faqs.a: Losar is the first day of the Tibetan lunar year, so the Gregorian date moves: usually in February, sometimes early March. Festivities run for several days, with the first three days the most important. Check the year's date with a monastery or your hotel, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can tourists visit monasteries during Losar?
faqs.a: Yes, respectfully. The monasteries at Ghoom are working religious places, and Losar is a family and prayer time. Visit in the morning, dress modestly, walk clockwise, remove shoes where asked and do not photograph inside prayer halls without permission. A small offering in the donation box is welcome.

faqs.q: Is there a cham mask dance at Ghoom for Losar?
faqs.a: Sometimes, but not every year or at every monastery. Some monasteries hold cham dances in the days before Losar as part of the year-end rites. Programmes change, so ask at the monastery office or at your homestay a few days ahead and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What food is eaten at Losar?
faqs.a: Khapse, crisp fried biscuits twisted into shapes, are the signature, along with butter tea, chang (a mild fermented millet or barley drink), momos and family feasts. A dough soup called guthuk is eaten in many Tibetan homes in the days just before Losar. Bakeries in Darjeeling sell khapse in the weeks before.

name: Dashain in the Darjeeling hills
when: Sep–Oct, 15 days ending at Kojagrata Purnima (lunar calendar)
summary: Dashain is the biggest festival of the Nepali-speaking hills, held over about fifteen days in September or October, at the same time as Durga Puja in the plains. Families gather, elders put red tika and green jamara on the young, and hill towns fill with visitors from Bengal.
body: Dashain celebrates the victory of the goddess Durga over evil, and in the Darjeeling hills it is the year's main homecoming. It begins on Ghatasthapana, when barley or maize seeds are planted in a dark corner of the house to grow into jamara, the pale yellow-green shoots used at the end of the festival. The most important day is Vijaya Dashami (Dashain tika), when elders place a mix of red vermilion, rice and curd on the foreheads of younger relatives and tuck jamara behind their ears with a blessing.

In Darjeeling town, Chowk Bazaar and the Mall are crowded, shops are busy, and many offices and schools close for the holidays. In the villages around Takdah, Tinchuley and Bijanbari, families travel home and bamboo swings (ping) have traditionally been raised for children. Kite flying was once a strong Dashain custom in the hills, and you still see it. Markets sell new clothes, goats and sweets in the days before tika, and families cook meat dishes and sel roti for the visitors who come to receive blessings. Many homes in the hills keep the jamara corner dark and watered for the full ten days.

For travellers, Dashain overlaps with the Bengali Puja holidays, the busiest weeks of the autumn season. Prices for rooms and reserved cars rise, and shared jeeps from Siliguri fill early. The weather is usually turning clear after the monsoon. Dates follow the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel. Homestays in the villages often welcome guests to watch the tika ceremony if you ask politely.
tips: Book rooms and toy train seats early: Dashain and Durga Puja bring peak crowds from Bengal.
If a homestay family invites you to tika day, dress neatly and accept the blessing with both hands open.
Allow extra time for jeeps on the main Dashain days, when drivers are also going home.

faqs.q: When is Dashain celebrated in Darjeeling?
faqs.a: In September or October, following the lunar calendar. Dashain lasts about fifteen days, from Ghatasthapana to Kojagrata Purnima, with Vijaya Dashami (tika day) the main day. It falls at the same time as Durga Puja in Kolkata, so the hills are busy with visitors. Check the year's dates before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Dashain a good time to visit Darjeeling?
faqs.a: It is lively and the weather is usually clearing after the monsoon, but it is also peak season. Rooms, reserved cars and toy train seats sell out and prices rise. If you come, book early and stay a little outside town, in Ghoom, Lamahatta or Takdah, where homestays are calmer.

Jamara are barley or maize shoots grown in the dark for about ten days from the first day of Dashain, so they come up pale yellow-green. On tika day elders tuck them behind the ears or in the hair of younger relatives with the red tika. They stand for health and a good harvest.

faqs.q: Are shops and transport open during Dashain?
faqs.a: Mostly yes, but with gaps. Many offices and schools close, some small shops shut on tika day, and fewer shared jeeps run on the main days as drivers go home. Tourist businesses in Darjeeling usually stay open. Plan travel days away from tika day and check current status before you travel.

name: Tihar, the festival of lights
when: Oct–Nov, five days around Diwali (lunar calendar)
summary: Tihar is the five-day festival of lights of the Nepali-speaking hills, held around Diwali. Each day honours someone: crows, dogs, cows, the goddess Lakshmi, and finally brothers on Bhai Tika. Evenings bring lamps, marigold garlands and groups singing Deusi and Bhailo from house to house.
body: Tihar arrives about two to three weeks after Dashain, in October or November. The first day honours crows (Kag Tihar), the second dogs (Kukur Tihar), when street and house dogs alike are given marigold garlands, a tika and a good meal. The third morning is for cows, and that evening for Lakshmi, goddess of wealth, when houses are lit with lamps and candles and doorways are painted with a path of colour to lead her in.

On the evenings of Tihar, groups of young people and neighbours go from house to house singing Bhailo (girls) and Deusi (boys), call-and-response songs that ask for blessings and gifts; the household answers with money, sel roti and fruit, and the groups often collect for a local cause. The last day, Bhai Tika, is when sisters place a seven-coloured tika on their brothers and give them garlands of makhamali flowers.

Sel roti, a ring-shaped fried rice bread, is made in quantity in every home. For visitors, Tihar is one of the warmest times to be in a homestay. The weather is usually clear and cold. Dates follow the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel. Bakeries and street stalls sell it too, and families send plates of it to neighbours. Outside the towns, villages light rows of small oil lamps and candles along paths and windows, which is a lovely sight from a homestay balcony on Lakshmi Puja night.
tips: Stay in a village homestay for Tihar if you can: you will see the lamps, the songs and the sel roti being made.
If a Deusi or Bhailo group sings at your homestay, a small cash gift is the custom.
Kukur Tihar is a good day for photographs of garlanded dogs, but ask owners before you approach.

faqs.q: Is Tihar the same as Diwali?
faqs.a: They fall at the same time and share the Lakshmi Puja night of lamps, but Tihar is the Nepali form of the festival and lasts five days. It adds days for crows, dogs and cows, the Deusi and Bhailo singing, and Bhai Tika, when sisters bless their brothers with a seven-coloured tika.

Kukur Tihar is the second day of Tihar, when dogs are honoured. Families put a marigold garland and a red tika on their dogs and feed them well, and many people do the same for street dogs. It honours the dog as a loyal companion and, in Hindu belief, a messenger of Yama.

They are the house-to-house songs of Tihar. Girls sing Bhailo, mostly on the Lakshmi Puja evening, and boys sing Deusi on the following nights. The singers bless the household in verse and the household replies with money and food, often sel roti. Groups often raise funds for a local club or cause.

faqs.q: When is Tihar celebrated in Darjeeling?
faqs.a: In October or November, over five days around Diwali, set by the lunar calendar. Lakshmi Puja, the night of lamps, is the brightest evening, and Bhai Tika the most family-centred day. Hotels in Darjeeling are busy, so book ahead and check current status before you travel.

name: Rabindra Jayanti at Mungpoo
when: Early May, 25 Baishakh in the Bengali calendar (usually 8 or 9 May)
summary: Mungpoo marks Tagore's birth anniversary at Rabindra Bhavan, the house where he stayed four times between 1938 and 1940 and where his birthday was celebrated in 1940. Expect songs, recitations and local school programmes rather than a large festival.
body: Rabindranath Tagore came to Mungpoo as the guest of Maitreyi Devi and her husband, Dr Manmohan Sen, who worked at the government quinine factory. He stayed in 1938, twice in 1939 and again in 1940, when he arrived on 21 April and his birthday was celebrated in the house. Maitreyi Devi later wrote about these visits in Mongpute Rabindranath, translated as Tagore by the Fireside. Tagore kept writing and painting during these stays.

The house is now Rabindra Bhavan, a small museum with his furniture, photographs and paintings. On 25 Baishakh, Tagore's birthday in the Bengali calendar, the village holds a programme there and in local schools: Rabindra Sangeet, poems in Bengali and Nepali, garlands at his portrait. Visitors from Darjeeling, Kalimpong and Kolkata sometimes come for the day. The house also keeps furniture he used, and the rooms are small and simple, much as Maitreyi Devi describes them.

This is a local commemoration, not a ticketed event, and its scale changes from year to year. Rabindra Bhavan has been closed for repairs at times. Check current status before you travel, ideally by asking a Darjeeling driver or a Mungpoo homestay a week ahead. There are no hotels to speak of in the village, so most visitors come for the day from Darjeeling, Kurseong or Kalimpong and leave before the afternoon mist.
tips: Arrive by mid-morning; programmes at Rabindra Bhavan usually happen in the first half of the day.
Combine the visit with a walk past the cinchona plantations, first planted here in 1864.
Read a few pages of Tagore by the Fireside before you go; it describes the very rooms you will stand in.

faqs.q: When is Rabindra Jayanti celebrated at Mungpoo?
faqs.a: On 25 Baishakh in the Bengali calendar, Tagore's birth anniversary, which usually falls on 8 or 9 May. The programme at Rabindra Bhavan and the local schools is generally held that morning. Its scale changes each year, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Why is Tagore's birthday celebrated in Mungpoo?
faqs.a: Because Tagore stayed in Mungpoo four times between 1938 and 1940, as a guest of Maitreyi Devi and Dr Manmohan Sen, and his birthday was celebrated there in 1940. Their house is now Rabindra Bhavan, a museum, and the village keeps his birthday as its own.

faqs.q: Is Rabindra Bhavan open on Rabindra Jayanti?
faqs.a: It is normally the centre of the day's programme, but the museum has been closed for repairs at times. Opening hours and access can change, so ask a Darjeeling driver, your homestay or the local tourism office before you travel, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do I reach Mungpoo for Rabindra Jayanti?
faqs.a: Most people come by reserved car from Darjeeling, Kurseong or Kalimpong, roughly two hours each way, for about ₹3,000–4,000 for the day. Shared jeeps run to Mungpoo less often, mainly from the Teesta side. Leave early: the programme is in the morning, and mist closes in by afternoon.
